title: Energy Tariff Types Explained: UK Tariff Cards
description: Fixed, variable, tracker, time-of-use, Economy 7, EV, prepay, green and export tariffs explained with simple cards, so you can pick the right UK energy deal.
intro: Every energy deal in Britain is one of a few tariff types. Pick the right type for how you live, then compare suppliers’ prices for it.

image.alt: A black and white electricity meter

cardText: Fixed, variable, tracker, time-of-use, EV, prepay and more.

blocks.title: Tariff cards
blocks.intro: Tap a filter to narrow it down.

items.title: Standard variable
items.text: The tariff you’re on if you never chose one or your fix ended. Rates are limited by the Ofgem price cap and change every three months.

items.title: Fixed tariff
items.text: Your unit rates and standing charges stay the same for the term. You still pay for what you use.

items.title: Prepayment
items.text: Top up before you use energy, by smart meter app, key or card. Ofgem says prepay currently pays the lowest cap rates.
specs: Can switch with up to £500 debt

items.title: Green / renewable
items.text: Electricity matched with renewable generation. Some suppliers buy certificates, others buy power directly from generators.

items.title: Lower standing charge
items.text: An Ofgem pilot from April 2026 with EDF, E.ON, Octopus and British Gas: lower daily charge, higher unit rate. Can suit very low users.

items.title: Tracker
items.text: Rates follow wholesale prices, typically changing daily, usually with a cap on the maximum. Needs a smart meter.

items.title: Time-of-use
items.text: Different prices at different times. Some have fixed peak and off-peak bands, others change every half hour (agile tariffs).

items.title: EV tariff
items.text: Very cheap overnight electricity windows for charging an electric car, sometimes for the whole home.

items.title: Heat pump tariff
items.text: Cheaper electricity for homes heating with a heat pump, either a flat discount or cheaper set times.

items.title: Economy 7 / Economy 10
items.text: Seven (or ten) hours of cheaper night electricity. Designed for storage heaters and hot water. Needs a multi-rate meter.

items.title: Export tariff (SEG)
items.text: Get paid for electricity your solar panels send to the grid. Larger suppliers must offer a Smart Export Guarantee tariff.

sections.h2: Which tariff type should you choose?
sections.html:
• You want certainty: a fixed tariff, ideally priced at or below the current price cap.
  • You think prices will fall: stay on standard variable or a tracker, and accept that rates can also rise.
  • You have an EV, battery or heat pump: a time-of-use, EV or heat pump tariff usually beats everything else if you can shift usage.
  • You use very little energy: look at the Ofgem lower standing charge pilot tariffs.
  • You have storage heaters: check you are on Economy 7 or 10, and that your heaters charge during the cheap hours.

Sources: Ofgem: lower standing charge tariffs, next steps · Ofgem: Smart Export Guarantee.

Every tariff has two parts. The unit rate is what you pay per kWh. The standing charge is a fixed daily amount that covers network and supplier costs, whether you use energy or not. A tariff with a low unit rate but a high standing charge can cost more if you use little energy, so always compare both for your own annual usage.

faqs.q: Are fixed tariffs cheaper than the price cap?
faqs.a: Sometimes. In August 2026 Ofgem said fixes were available at £100 or more below the October cap. Prices change daily, so compare any fix with the current cap and with forecasts for the next one.

faqs.q: Can I leave a fixed tariff early?
faqs.a: Yes, but you may pay an exit fee. Suppliers can’t charge exit fees if you switch in the last 49 days of a fixed deal.

faqs.q: Do I need a smart meter for a time-of-use tariff?
faqs.a: Yes. Tracker, agile, EV and most time-of-use tariffs need a smart meter that sends half-hourly readings.
